claims.text: Pulsed Thermal Annealing can control phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs more effectively than conventional heat treatments.
Repeated thermal pulses perturb the free-energy landscape.
Pulsed Thermal Annealing overcomes sluggish phase-transformation kinetics in these HEAs.
Pulsed Thermal Annealing traps metastable phases in these HEAs.
The initial Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA is in an as-processed, multiphase state.
The starting alloy exhibits complex and sluggish phase transformations.
The proposed treatment uses 10 cycles of approximately 1000°C for one minute followed by quenching at approximately 80°C/s.
An inert atmosphere prevents oxidation during the proposed treatment.
Repeated thermal cycling enables faster diffusion.
Repeated thermal cycling promotes nucleation events.
Each thermal pulse temporarily equilibrates the microstructure at high temperature.
Each thermal pulse permits short-range atomic rearrangements and phase nucleation.
Rapid quenching freezes the microstructure before equilibrium is reached.
Repeating the pulse-and-quench cycle selectively promotes phase transformations otherwise hindered by sluggish kinetics.
The proposed treatment produces a more uniform and tailored distribution of constituent phases.
The resulting microstructure may have improved mechanical properties relative to conventional equilibration methods.
Traditional equilibrium-based heat treatments typically produce inconsistent and less-controlled phase distributions in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs because of kinetic hindrances.
The effectiveness of the proposed method may be limited to conditions near 1000°C and an approximately 80°C/s quench rate.
The proposed method may not extrapolate to HEA systems with different compositions or thermal responses.
